line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 c3
teaches: Choosing an opening line is a practical decision, not only an objective one — the knight's modest development square costs a little activity and buys an enormous saving in theory, because the c-pawn keeps its job. When the chain forms, that pawn props the base and the whole structure holds itself with no memorisation required.
explains: The pawn steps to c3 and defends the pawn on d4, the base of the chain — possible only because the knight developed to d2 instead of onto the c-pawn's square. The centre is now held by pawns, and the pieces are free to find their standard posts at leisure.

line: e4 e6 d4 d5 Nd2 Nf6 e5 Nfd7 c3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 Ngf3 Qb6 Ng1 Qd8 Ne2 Qb6 Nf3 Qc7 Bd2 Qd8 Nc1 Be7 O-O a5 a4
teaches: When your play is on one wing, spend a single pawn move to freeze the other. The rook-pawn's advance takes away the square the enemy pawns need to start rolling, and the counterplay that would have arrived in five moves never arrives at all.
explains: The pawn goes to a4 and takes b5 away, so the queenside pawns opposite have no lever to advance with — their storm needs that square and it is gone. The kingside plans can now be prepared without a clock ticking on the other side of the board.
